prs.title: fix[dropWhile, dropRightWhile, some]: normalize the predicate like lodash
prs.author: Archibald1948
prs.request:
fix[dropWhile, dropRightWhile, some]: normalize the predicate like lodash

## The difference (as code)

`es-toolkit/compat`'s `dropWhile`, `dropRightWhile` and `some` return `undefined` for a boolean predicate, and `dropWhile` / `dropRightWhile` treat a `null` predicate as "match everything" instead of `identity`:

```js
dropWhile([1, 2, 3], true);                   // lodash: [1, 2, 3]      es-toolkit: undefined
dropWhile([{ true: 1 }, { true: 0 }], true);  // lodash: [{ true: 0 }]  es-toolkit: undefined
dropRightWhile([1, 2, 3], true);              // lodash: [1, 2, 3]      es-toolkit: undefined
dropRightWhile([{ false: 1 }], false);        // lodash: []             es-toolkit: undefined
some([1, 2, 3], true);                        // lodash: false          es-toolkit: undefined
some([{ false: 1 }], false);                  // lodash: true           es-toolkit: undefined

dropWhile([0, 1, 2], null);                   // lodash: [0, 1, 2]      es-toolkit: []
dropRightWhile([1, 2, 0], null);              // lodash: [1, 2, 0]      es-toolkit: []
```

`some` is declared to return `boolean`, so this also breaks its own signature.

## Cause

Lodash normalizes every shorthand through `baseIteratee`, which has a nullish check and a catch-all:

```js
function baseIteratee(value) {
  if (typeof value == 'function') return value;
  if (value == null) return identity;          // <- nullish
  if (typeof value == 'object') {
    return isArray(value) ? baseMatchesProperty(value[0], value[1]) : baseMatches(value);
  }
  return property(value);                      // <- catch-all
}
```

`es-toolkit/compat` already mirrors both in `iteratee()`, and most compat collection functions route their predicate through it. `dropWhile`, `dropRightWhile` and `some` instead hand-roll the same switch, and the hand-rolled copy is missing both pieces.

**1. The switch is not total.** It enumerates the primitive cases rather than using `default:`:

```js
case 'number':
case 'symbol':
case 'string': {
  return dropWhileToolkit(arr, property(predicate));
}
```

A `boolean` predicate matches no case, so control falls out of the bottom of the switch and the function implicitly returns `undefined`. (`dropRightWhile` additionally omits `'symbol'`.)

**2. A default parameter does not cover `null`.** `dropWhile` and `dropRightWhile` declare `predicate: ListIteratee<T> = identity`, but a default parameter only applies to `undefined`. A `null` predicate reaches the switch, hits `typeof null === 'object'`, and becomes `matches(null)` — which matches every element, so every element is dropped.

## Changes

1. Replace the enumerated primitive cases with `default:` so each switch is total and lands on the same catch-all `iteratee()` already uses:

[diff-like code block removed]

2. Normalize a nullish predicate with `predicate ?? identity`, the way the neighbouring `takeWhile` already does:

```js
- export function dropWhile<T>(array: ArrayLike<T> | null | undefined, predicate: ListIteratee<T> = identity): T[] {
+ export function dropWhile<T>(array: ArrayLike<T> | null | undefined, predicate?: ListIteratee<T>): T[] {
    if (!isArrayLike(array)) {
      return [];
    }

-   return dropWhileImpl(toArray(array), predicate);
+   return dropWhileImpl(toArray(array), predicate ?? identity);
  }
```

The parameter stays optional, so the public type is unchanged. No other branch is touched.

## Verification

Differential run against `lodash@4.18.1` over 8 functions x 9 collections x 9 predicate values (648 combinations):

| | mismatches |
| --- | --- |
| before | 158 / 648 |
| after | 67 / 648 |

Fixed: 40 in `dropWhile`, 40 in `dropRightWhile`, 36 in `some`. The five untouched sibling functions (`every`, `filter`, `find`, `takeWhile`, `takeRightWhile`) produce a byte-identical mismatch list before and after.

All 67 remaining mismatches are the single predicate `0n`, where **lodash itself throws** `TypeError: Cannot mix BigInt and other types` (its `toKey` evaluates `1 / value` on a BigInt). After this change the three functions return a value there — exactly like `filter` (8), `find` (8), `every` (9), `takeWhile` (8) and `takeRightWhile` (8) already do — so that behaviour is pre-existing across compat and is neither introduced nor changed here.

Regression tests were added to all three spec files. On `main` they fail with:

```
AssertionError: expected undefined to deeply equal [ 1, 2, 3 ]
AssertionError: expected undefined to be false // Object.is equality
AssertionError: expected [] to deeply equal [ 1, 2, +0 ]
```

Full suite: 699 files, 4889 passed / 2 skipped. `tsc --noEmit` clean, `yarn lint` 0 errors.

## Benchmarks

Interleaved A/B (`fix`, then `main`, five times alternating, so machine drift affects both sides equally), median of the five paired per-round deltas:

| benchmark | delta |
| --- | --- |
| `es-toolkit/compat/dropWhile` | +6.7% |
| `es-toolkit/compat/dropWhile` — largeArray | -4.1% |
| `es-toolkit (compat)/dropRightWhile` | +7.9% |
| `es-toolkit (compat)/dropRightWhile` — largeArray | +0.8% |
| `es-toolkit/some` (this bench imports from `es-toolkit/compat`) | +8.4% |
| `es-toolkit/some` — largeArray | +1.0% |
| *control* `lodash/dropWhile` (untouched) | +0.1% |
| *control* `lodash/dropRightWhile` (untouched) | +1.0% |
| *control* `lodash/some` (untouched) | +0.4% |
| *control* `es-toolkit/dropWhile` (untouched, non-compat) | +4.6% |
| *control* `es-toolkit/dropRightWhile` (untouched, non-compat) | -1.7% |

No regression. The untouched controls in the same runs move by -1.7% to +4.6% and individual rounds vary by more than +/-10%, so I am not claiming a real speedup — the honest reading is that these are within this machine's noise. The one pattern that is at least consistent with the change is that the per-call benchmarks trend slightly positive while the `largeArray` ones do not, which is what you would expect from replacing three sequential `case` string comparisons with a single `default`.

prs.title: fix(countBy): return a plain object from compat countBy
prs.author: MFA-G
prs.request:
fix(countBy): return a plain object from compat countBy

## Summary

`countBy` from `es-toolkit/compat` returns an object with a `null` prototype, while lodash returns a plain object. Anything the consumer does with the result that touches `Object.prototype` behaves differently from lodash — and in one case throws.

```ts
import { countBy } from 'es-toolkit/compat';
import lodash from 'lodash';

const words = ['one', 'two', 'three'];

Object.getPrototypeOf(lodash.countBy(words, 'length')); // Object.prototype
Object.getPrototypeOf(countBy(words, 'length'));        // null

const counts = countBy(words, 'length');
counts instanceof Object;                // false  (lodash: true)
typeof counts.hasOwnProperty;            // 'undefined'  (lodash: 'function')
`${counts}`;                             // TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value
```

The `TypeError` is the sharpest edge: interpolating the result into a string, or anything else that invokes `toString` — a logger, a template, `String(counts)` — throws on a value that works under lodash. `counts instanceof Object` returning `false` is the kind of thing a downstream type guard trips over.

It is also inconsistent within compat itself. The nullish-collection branch already returns `{}`, so `countBy(null)` has `Object.prototype` while `countBy([])` does not. And the neighbouring aggregators, `groupBy` and `keyBy`, both return plain objects — `countBy` is the only one of the three that does not.

I found this with a differential fuzz of `es-toolkit/compat` against lodash across ~10,500 calls; `countBy` accounted for 112 of the 136 mismatches, all of them this one prototype difference.

## Changes

- `src/compat/array/countBy.ts`: build the result on a plain object instead of `Object.create(null)`.
  - Counts are read with `Object.hasOwn` rather than `result[key] ?? 0`, so an inherited member such as `constructor` or `toString` is not mistaken for an existing count. The existing `should only add values to own, not inherited, properties` test covers this and still passes.
  - A `__proto__` key is written with `Object.defineProperty` rather than assignment, so it becomes an own property instead of replacing the prototype — matching lodash, which counts `__proto__` as an ordinary key.
- `src/compat/array/countBy.spec.ts`: two tests, both failing before the change.
  - the result is a plain object: prototype, `instanceof Object`, `hasOwnProperty`, string interpolation, and the empty-collection case.
  - a `__proto__` key is counted as an own property and leaves the prototype intact.

The main `es-toolkit` `countBy` is unaffected; it already returns a plain object.

prs.title: fix[pull, pullAll, pullAllBy, remove]: handle nullish inputs like lodash
prs.author: Archibald1948
prs.request:
fix[pull, pullAll, pullAllBy, remove]: handle nullish inputs like lodash

## The difference (as code)

`pull`, `pullAll`, `pullAllBy` and `remove` in `es-toolkit/compat` throw on a nullish array, where lodash returns it unchanged:

```js
pull(null, 1);             // lodash: null        es-toolkit: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'length')
pull(undefined, 1);        // lodash: undefined   es-toolkit: TypeError
pullAll(null, [1]);        // lodash: null        es-toolkit: TypeError
pullAllBy(undefined, [1]); // lodash: undefined   es-toolkit: TypeError
remove(null, isEven);      // lodash: []          es-toolkit: TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'slice')
```

`pullAllBy` also throws when `values` is left out, even though its signature declares `values?` as optional:

```js
pullAllBy([1, 2, 1]);      // lodash: [1, 2, 1]   es-toolkit: TypeError: undefined is not iterable
```

This is the kind of call that shows up in real code, e.g. `pull(user.tags, 'draft')` where `tags` may be missing.

## Cause

Lodash puts one guard in front of the whole family:

```js
function pullAll(array, values) {
  return (array && array.length && values && values.length)
    ? basePullAll(array, values)
    : array;
}
// pullAllBy / pullAllWith: the same guard. pull = baseRest(pullAll).

function remove(array, predicate) {
  var result = [];
  if (!(array && array.length)) {
    return result;
  }
  // ...
}
```

In compat, only `pullAllWith` has an equivalent guard:

```js
if (array?.length == null || values?.length == null) {
  return array;
}
```

The other three do not:

- `pull` forwards straight to the strict `es-toolkit` `pull`, which reads `arr.length`.
- `pullAll` guards `values` (#1962) but not `array`.
- `pullAllBy` guards neither and starts with `Array.from(valuesToRemove)`.
- `remove` forwards straight to the strict `es-toolkit` `remove`, which calls `arr.slice()`.

## Changes

Use `pullAllWith`'s guard in `pull`, `pullAll` and `pullAllBy`, and return `[]` from `remove` for the same condition (the value lodash's `remove` returns):

```js
// pull
if (arr?.length == null) {
  return arr;
}

// pullAll, pullAllBy
if (arr?.length == null || valuesToRemove?.length == null) {
  return arr;
}

// remove
if (arr?.length == null) {
  return [];
}
```

In `pullAll` this replaces the existing `isNil(valuesToRemove)` check, which the new guard already covers.

Two side effects, both toward lodash, called out so they are not a surprise:

1. **Values without a `length` are no longer mutated.** Previously `pull({ a: 1 }, 1)` returned the object with a `length: 0` property stamped onto it. It is now returned untouched, as in lodash.
2. **A `Set` passed as `values` is now ignored.** Previously `pullAll([1, 2, 3], new Set([1]))` spread the Set with `Array.from` and returned `[2, 3]`. Lodash (and compat's own `pullAllWith`) only read array-like `values`, so it now returns `[1, 2, 3]`. A `Set` is not assignable to the declared `ArrayLike<T>`, so this is only reachable from plain JS or through a cast.

## Verification

Focused grid against `lodash@4.18.1` (nullish, empty and non-empty arrays x omitted / `undefined` / `null` / `[]` / `[1]` values, 92 calls, comparing both the return value and the mutated array):

| | mismatches |
| --- | --- |
| before | 44 / 92 (all "es-toolkit throws, lodash returns") |
| after | 0 / 92 |

Broad sweep over the five functions (`pull`, `pullAll`, `pullAllBy`, `pullAllWith`, `remove`) with every 1- and 2-argument combination of a 35-value pool (6,300 calls):

| | mismatches |
| --- | --- |
| before | 3,698 |
| after | 751 |

2,947 calls fixed, **0 calls that matched before and mismatch now**, and the remaining 751 are byte-identical before and after. They are all strings, functions or array-like objects passed as the array (e.g. `pullAll('', [])`: lodash returns early on empty `values`, while compat carries on and throws when it assigns `length` on the string primitive). `pullAllBy`'s remaining set is exactly the same as `pullAllWith`'s, the sibling that already had this guard, so those are pre-existing and out of scope here.

Regression tests were added to all four spec files. On `main` they fail with:

```
TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'length')
TypeError: Cannot read properties of null (reading 'slice')
TypeError: undefined is not iterable (cannot read property Symbol(Symbol.iterator))
AssertionError: expected { a: 1, length: +0 } to deeply equal { a: 1 }
AssertionError: expected [ 2, 3 ] to deeply equal [ 1, 2, 3 ]
```

Full suite: 714 files, 5037 passed / 2 skipped. `tsc --noEmit` clean, `yarn lint` 0 errors (no new warnings in the touched files), type-tests pass.

## Benchmarks

The guard is one optional-chained `length` check per call. Interleaved A/B (`fix`, then `main`, five alternating rounds), median of the paired per-round deltas:

| benchmark | main (hz) | fix (hz) | delta |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `pull` — array size 100 | 546,614 | 548,697 | +0.5% |
| `pull` — array size 1,000 | 47,913 | 47,876 | +0.9% |
| `pull` — array size 10,000 | 2,736 | 2,720 | +0.1% |
| `pullAllBy` | 3,707,047 | 3,698,570 | -0.3% |
| *control* `lodash/pull` — size 100 / 1,000 / 10,000 | | | -0.9% / -0.2% / +0.4% |
| *control* `lodash/pullAllBy` | | | -0.1% |

All within +/-1%, the same band as the untouched lodash controls, so no measurable change. (`pull.bench.ts` labels its compat benchmark `es-toolkit/pull`, but it imports from `es-toolkit/compat`.) `pullAll` and `remove` have no benchmark files.

prs.title: fix[xorBy, xorWith]: ignore the iteratee and comparator for a single array like lodash
prs.author: Archibald1948
prs.request:
fix[xorBy, xorWith]: ignore the iteratee and comparator for a single array like lodash

> [!NOTE]
> **Update after merge — the description below does not match the merged code.**
>
> This PR was merged with the maintainer's commit d4afbfc2 on top, so the final code in both functions is:
>
> [diff-like code block removed]
>
> The following parts of this description refer to a later revision of mine that was **never pushed** (its push was rejected because d4afbfc2 had already landed): the `uniqToolkit(flattenArrayLike(arrays))` code under "Changes", the statement that the current code reads array-likes by index, the array-like regression tests, and the benchmark table.
>
> What still holds for the merged code: the differential results (0 / 1,260 mismatches against lodash for `xor`, `xorBy` and `xorWith`) and the correction about the first revision.
>
> One difference remains, and it is the same as compat's own `uniq` and `xor`: the merged code reads array-likes through `Array.from`, so an array-like whose `Symbol.iterator` disagrees with its indices still differs from lodash (`['b']` instead of `['a']` for the example below).

---

## The difference (as code)

Given a single array, `xorBy` and `xorWith` in `es-toolkit/compat` apply the iteratee / comparator, while lodash ignores it:

```js
xorBy([2.1, 2.3], Math.floor);        // lodash: [2.1, 2.3]              es-toolkit: [2.1]
xorBy([{ x: 1 }, { x: 1 }], 'x');     // lodash: [{ x: 1 }, { x: 1 }]    es-toolkit: [{ x: 1 }]
xorWith([{ a: 1 }, { a: 1 }], isEqual); // lodash: [{ a: 1 }, { a: 1 }]  es-toolkit: [{ a: 1 }]
xorWith([1, 2, 3], (a, b) => a === b);  // lodash: [1, 2, 3]             es-toolkit: [1]
```

The last one is the clearest: with `(a, b) => a === b` nothing in `[1, 2, 3]` is a duplicate, yet compat collapses the array to `[1]`.

## Cause

`baseXor` short-circuits before the iteratee and the comparator are ever used:

```js
function baseXor(arrays, iteratee, comparator) {
  var length = arrays.length;
  if (length < 2) {
    return length ? baseUniq(arrays[0]) : [];   // <- neither argument is passed on
  }
  // ...
  return baseUniq(baseFlatten(result, 1), iteratee, comparator);
}
```

Both `xorBy` and `xorWith` route through it (`baseXor(arrayFilter(arrays, isArrayLikeObject), getIteratee(iteratee, 2))` and `baseXor(..., undefined, comparator)`), so for one array lodash falls back to a plain `baseUniq`: SameValueZero de-duplication with `-0` normalized, and no iteratee.

`es-toolkit/compat` instead always builds the union / intersection / difference chain, which does apply the iteratee or comparator:

```js
const union = unionBy(...arrays, mapper);
const intersections = windowed(arrays, 2).map(([arr1, arr2]) => intersectionBy(arr1, arr2, mapper));

return differenceBy(union, unionBy(...intersections, mapper), mapper);
```

With a single array `windowed(arrays, 2)` is empty, so this reduces to `unionBy(array, mapper)` — a de-duplication *by the iteratee*, which is not what lodash does.

## Changes

Return early when fewer than two array-like arguments remain, reproducing `baseUniq(arrays[0])`:

```js
const arrays = values.filter(isArrayLikeObject) as [any];

// With fewer than two arrays lodash's `baseXor` returns `baseUniq(arrays[0])`,
// dropping the iteratee. `baseUniq` reads elements by index and de-duplicates
// with SameValueZero, normalizing `-0`, which is what a `Set` does.
if (arrays.length < 2) {
  return uniqToolkit(flattenArrayLike(arrays));
}
```

Two details matter here, both of which an earlier revision of this PR got wrong:

1. **Read by index.** `baseUniq` reads `array[i]`. `flattenArrayLike` (the helper `unionBy` / `unionWith` already use) copies by index, so an array-like whose `Symbol.iterator` disagrees with its indices is still read the lodash way.
2. **One `Set`.** The strict `uniq` is `[...new Set(arr)]`, which is SameValueZero with `-0` normalized and first-occurrence order — the same result as `baseUniq`, with a single allocation.

With no arrays at all, `flattenArrayLike([])` is `[]`, matching `length ? baseUniq(arrays[0]) : []`. The two-or-more-array path is untouched.

## Verification

Differential against `lodash@4.18.1`, every 1- and 2-argument combination of a 35-value pool (1,260 calls per function):

| | `xorBy` | `xorWith` | `xor` (untouched) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| before | 102 / 1,260 | 4 / 1,260 | 0 / 1,260 |
| after | **0 / 1,260** | **0 / 1,260** | 0 / 1,260 |

A focused set of 20 calls (single array with and without an iteratee, `-0`, `NaN`, duplicates, no arrays at all, and two-array calls that must not change) goes from 9 mismatches to 0.

**Correction to the first revision.** It delegated to `xor(...arrays)` and I wrote that no previously-matching call mismatched afterwards. Copilot's review pointed out that `xor` reads through `Array.from`, i.e. the iterator, and that did regress an array-like whose iterator disagrees with its indices — a case my value pool did not contain:

```js
const arrayLike = { 0: 'a', length: 1, *[Symbol.iterator]() { yield 'b'; } };

xorBy(arrayLike, x => x);
// lodash: ['a']   main: ['a']   first revision: ['b']   now: ['a']
```

The current code reads by index, and both spec files now pin this object.

Regression tests were added to both spec files. On `main` the single-array tests fail with:

```
AssertionError: expected [ 2.1 ] to deeply equal [ 2.1, 2.3 ]
AssertionError: expected [ { a: 1 } ] to deeply equal [ { a: 1 }, { a: 1 } ]
```

and on the first revision the array-like tests fail with:

```
AssertionError: expected [ 'b' ] to deeply equal [ 'a' ]
```

Full suite: 714 files, 5041 passed / 2 skipped. `tsc --noEmit` clean, `yarn lint` 0 errors (no new warnings in the touched files), type-tests pass.

## Benchmarks

Interleaved A/B (`fix`, then `main`, five alternating rounds), median of the paired per-round deltas. The existing benchmarks only cover the two-array path, so I added a temporary local benchmark for the single-array path. Before every run the Vite dependency cache was cleared, and after every run I checked the pre-bundled `es-toolkit/compat` for which implementation had actually been measured (10/10 matched the intended side).

| benchmark | main (hz) | fix (hz) | delta |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| *single array* `xorBy`, 10 items | 967,116 | 2,767,538 | **+184%** |
| *single array* `xorBy`, 1,000 items | 12,646 | 35,369 | **+178%** |
| *single array* `xorWith`, 10 items | 2,150,657 | 2,573,311 | **+20%** |
| *single array* `xorWith`, 1,000 items | 1,705 | 35,744 | **+1,997%** |
| `xorBy` (2 arrays) | 1,105,968 | 1,078,839 | -2.0% |
| `xorBy` — largeArray | 287 | 287 | +0.1% |
| `xorWith` (2 arrays) | 1,710,252 | 1,691,604 | +1.0% |
| `xorWith` — largeArray | 1.0 | 1.0 | +0.2% |
| *control* `lodash/xorBy` (2 arrays / largeArray) | | | -0.5% / +0.3% |
| *control* `lodash/xorWith` (2 arrays / largeArray) | | | -1.0% / -0.1% |

The single-array path is faster across the board, most of all with a comparator on larger arrays, where it no longer runs the O(n²) `unionWith` / `differenceWith` chain. The only code added to the two-array path is the `arrays.length < 2` check; small two-array `xorBy` came out 2.0% slower with all five rounds negative (-0.9% to -3.2%), slightly outside the controls' band, so I'm noting it rather than calling it noise.

**About the benchmark table in the first revision:** those numbers showed no difference on any path, and they were wrong. The runs did not clear Vite's pre-bundled dependency cache, so both sides measured the same cached build. That is also how the xor-based version's 33% slowdown for a 10-item single array with a comparator went unnoticed; the cache-cleared runs caught it, which is why the current code uses `uniq` instead of `xor`.

prs.title: fix[forEach, forEachRight, forIn, forInRight, forOwn, forOwnRight, reduce, reduceRight]: resolve the iteratee like lodash
prs.author: Archibald1948
prs.request:
fix[forEach, forEachRight, forIn, forInRight, forOwn, forOwnRight, reduce, reduceRight]: resolve the iteratee like lodash

## The difference (as code)

The iteration functions below call their `iteratee` directly, so anything that is not a function throws, where lodash resolves it the way every other collection method does:

```js
forEach([1, 2, 3], null);                 // lodash: [1, 2, 3]        es-toolkit: TypeError: callback is not a function
forOwn({ a: { x: 1 } }, 'x');             // lodash: { a: { x: 1 } }  es-toolkit: TypeError: iteratee is not a function
reduce([1, 2, 3], null);                  // lodash: 1                es-toolkit: TypeError: iteratee is not a function
reduce([{ a: 1 }, { a: 1 }], { a: 1 });   // lodash: true             es-toolkit: TypeError: iteratee is not a function
```

Affected: `forEach`, `forEachRight`, `forIn`, `forInRight`, `forOwn`, `forOwnRight`, `reduce`, `reduceRight` (and the `each` / `eachRight` aliases).

Shorthands are not just tolerated by lodash, they are honoured. In the `forEach` family a property shorthand that returns `false` stops the iteration, exactly like a callback returning `false`:

```js
let visited = 0;
const array = [{ a: false }, { get a() { visited++; return true; } }];

forEach(array, 'a');
// lodash: stops at the first element, visited === 0
// es-toolkit: TypeError
```

## Cause

In lodash all eight go through `getIteratee`, i.e. `baseIteratee`:

```js
function forEach(collection, iteratee) {
  var func = isArray(collection) ? arrayEach : baseEach;
  return func(collection, getIteratee(iteratee, 3));
}

function forOwn(object, iteratee) {
  return object && baseForOwn(object, getIteratee(iteratee, 3));
}

function reduce(collection, iteratee, accumulator) {
  // ...
  return func(collection, getIteratee(iteratee, 4), accumulator, initAccum, baseEach);
}
```

In compat they only default the parameter to `identity` and then call it, so `null` (not covered by a default parameter) and every shorthand reach a call on a non-function:

```js
export function forOwn(object, iteratee = identity) {
  // ...
  if (iteratee(iterable[key], key, iterable) === false) {
```

`es-toolkit/compat` already has the `baseIteratee` equivalent, `iteratee()`, and `filter` / `partition` already resolve their predicate with it:

```js
predicate = iteratee(predicate);
```

## Changes

Resolve the iteratee once per call, right after the early return, the same way `filter` does:

[diff-like code block removed]

`iteratee()` returns a function argument unchanged and maps `null` / `undefined` to `identity`, so existing callers see no difference. Each file gains one import and one line.

## Verification

Focused grid against `lodash@4.18.1`: 10 functions x 6 collections x 8 iteratee values (omitted, `undefined`, `null`, `0`, `'a'`, `{ a: 1 }`, `['a', 1]`, `true`), 480 calls:

| | mismatches |
| --- | --- |
| before | 240 / 480 (every one "lodash returns, es-toolkit throws") |
| after | **0 / 480** |

Broad sweep, every 1- and 2-argument combination of a 35-value pool (1,260 calls per function):

| | `forEach` family (8 incl. aliases) | `reduce` / `reduceRight` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| before | 352 / 1,260 each | 224 / 1,260 each |
| after | **0 / 1,260 each** | 21 / 1,260 each |

No call that matched before mismatches now. The 21 left for `reduce` / `reduceRight` are all `[]`, `Map` or `Set` used as the iteratee. Those used to throw; now they return what compat's shared `iteratee()` produces for those values, which is the same known difference `filter`, `find` and the other shorthand-taking functions already have against lodash — out of scope here. The `forEach` family shows no such residue because it only looks at whether the result is `false`.

Regression tests were added to all eight spec files (14 tests). On `main` they fail with:

```
TypeError: iteratee is not a function
TypeError: callback is not a function
```

Full suite: 714 files, 5053 passed / 2 skipped. `tsc --noEmit` clean, `yarn lint` 0 errors (no new warnings in the touched files), type-tests pass.

## Benchmarks

The change adds one `iteratee()` call per invocation (a `null` check and a `typeof` switch), independent of collection size.

Interleaved A/B (`fix`, then `main`, seven alternating rounds) on the three hottest benchmarks. Before every run the Vite dependency cache was cleared, and after every run I checked the pre-bundled `es-toolkit/compat` for which implementation had actually been measured (14/14 matched the intended side). Each compat row is divided by the lodash row of the same group in the same round to cancel machine drift; the table shows the median of the seven normalized deltas.

| benchmark | normalized delta |
| --- | ---: |
| `forEach` | -0.8% |
| `forEach` — largeArray | -3.8% |
| `forEach` — object | 0.0% |
| `forEach` — string | -2.4% |
| `forOwn` | -0.8% |
| `reduce` | -4.7% |
| `reduce` — large array | -1.1% |

I want to be upfront that these runs were noisy: the machine was under other load at the time (load average around 5 on 8 cores), and individual rounds swung by up to +/-50% even on the lodash controls. The large-array rows are the clearest indicator of the noise floor — a constant per-call cost cannot move a benchmark that spends ~75µs per call by 3.8% — so I read this as no consistent effect within roughly +/-5%, not as a measured slowdown. `filter` and `partition` already resolve their predicate the same way. prs.title: fix(words): match titlecase letters, aligning with lodash
prs.author: mariazuheros
prs.request:
fix(words): match titlecase letters, aligning with lodash

## Summary

`words` (and everything built on it: `camelCase`, `kebabCase`, `snakeCase`, `startCase`, `lowerCase`, `upperCase`) recognized uppercase (`\p{Lu}`) and lowercase (`\p{Ll}`) letters, but not **titlecase** letters (Unicode category `Lt`). As a result, titlecase letters were silently dropped instead of being treated as part of a word, which diverges from lodash.

Affected characters are the Latin digraphs `ǅ ǈ ǋ ǲ` and the Greek titlecase forms `ᾈ..ᾯ` (31 code points in total).

```ts
words('ǅ');        // es-toolkit: []              lodash: ['ǅ']
words('fooǅBar');  // es-toolkit: ['foo', 'Bar']  lodash: ['fooǅ', 'Bar']
```

## Fix

Add `\p{Lt}` to the misc-letter class in the Unicode word pattern:

[diff-like code block removed]

This mirrors lodash's `rsMisc`, where a titlecase letter is valid in both the upper and lower word positions. I verified the placement differentially against lodash 4.x: putting `\p{Lt}` in the misc class reproduces lodash exactly across all 31 titlecase code points and mixed strings (0 mismatches), whereas treating it as a plain lowercase letter diverges on boundary cases.

Because `camelCase`, `kebabCase`, `snakeCase`, `lowerCase` and `upperCase` all build on `words`, they line up with lodash for these characters too.

## Tests

Added a `should match titlecase letters` case in `words.spec.ts` (red-green verified). Updated the `es-toolkit/compat` `camelCase` bundle-size snapshot, which grows by 7 bytes from the added property escape.

prs.title: fix(compat/words): keep combining marks attached to the letter they modify
prs.author: ssi02014
prs.request: fix(compat/words): keep combining marks attached to the letter they modify ## Summary `es-toolkit/compat`'s `words` drops or splits on Unicode combining marks (`\p{M}`), so decomposed (NFD) text is not tokenized the way Lodash tokenizes it. The Unicode word pattern matched `\p{Lu}` / `\p{Ll}` alone, and its "misc" branch only allowed a combining mark after an `\p{Lm}`/`\p{Lo}` base. A combining mark that follows a cased letter therefore matched nothing: it either ended the word early and was swallowed, or it broke one word into two. Lodash does not have this problem because its `rsMisc` is a negated character class that already contains combining marks, so a mark following a letter keeps the match going. ```ts const str = 'café'; const nfdStr = str.normalize('NFD'); // 'cafe\u0301', length: 5 const nfcStr = str.normalize('NFC'); // 'caf\u00E9', length: 4 _.words(nfcStr); // lodash → ['café'] _.words(nfdStr); // lodash → ['café'] words(nfcStr); // es-toolkit/compat(before) → ['café'] ✅ words(nfdStr); // es-toolkit/compat(before) → ['cafe'] ← the accent is dropped ``` ```ts const str = 'abćdef'; const nfdStr = str.normalize('NFD'); // 'abc\u0301def', length: 7 const nfcStr = str.normalize('NFC'); // 'ab\u0107def', length: 6 _.words(nfcStr); // lodash → ['abćdef'] _.words(nfdStr); // lodash → ['abćdef'] words(nfcStr); // es-toolkit/compat(before) → ['abćdef'] ✅ words(nfdStr); // es-toolkit/compat(before) → ['abc', 'def'] ← split at the mark ``` Full comparison on decomposed input: | input (NFD) | lodash | compat (before) | compat (after) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 'café' | `['café']` | `['cafe']` | `['café']` | | 'naïve' | `['naïve']` | `['nai', 've']` | `['naïve']` | | 'Nguyễn' | `['Nguyễn']` | `['Nguye', 'n']` | `['Nguyễn']` | | 'abćdef' | `['abćdef']` | `['abc', 'def']` | `['abćdef']` | | 'été 2024' | `['été', '2024']` | `['e', 'te', '2024']` | `['été', '2024']` | 💡An accented character can be encoded two ways that are visually identical but are different strings in JavaScript: - NFC (precomposed): é = U+00E9 — one code point - NFD (decomposed): é = e (U+0065) + U+0301 (COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT) — two code points The decomposed form is always the one that breaks. The NFC spellings(`caf\u00E9` and `na\u00EFve`) pass the same pattern cleanly, so this bug only reproduces depending on which normalization form the input arrived in. ## Question `src/string/words` (the non-compat entry point) has the same behavior today — it uses `CASE_SPLIT_PATTERN`, which also matches `\p{Lu}`/`\p{Ll}` without allowing trailing combining marks, so `words('cafe\u0301')` splits or drops the mark there as well. Since that function is not bound by Lodash compatibility, should it match Lodash here too, or is keeping the current behavior intentional? ```ts const str = 'café'; const nfdStr = str.normalize('NFD'); // 'cafe\u0301', length: 5 const nfcStr = str.normalize('NFC'); // 'caf\u00E9', length: 4 words(nfcStr); // es-toolkit/words(before) → ['café'] ✅ words(nfdStr); // es-toolkit/words(before) → ['cafe'] ← the accent is dropped ``` ```ts const str = 'abćdef'; const nfdStr = str.normalize('NFD'); // 'abc\u0301def', length: 7 const nfcStr = str.normalize('NFC'); // 'ab\u0107def', length: 6 words(nfcStr); // es-toolkit/compat(before) → ['abćdef'] ✅ words(nfdStr); // es-toolkit/words(before) → ['abc', 'def'] ← split at the mark ``` Based on the existing test suite, retaining accents appears to be the intended design. Therefore, handling NFD-formatted strings properly seems appropriate: ```ts it('should match accented letters', () => { expect(words('Lunedì 18 Set')).toEqual(['Lunedì', '18', 'Set']); }); ``` ```ts it('should match accented letters', () => { const str = 'Lunedì'; const nfdStr = str.normalize('NFD'); // 'Lunedi\u0301' const nfcStr = str.normalize('NFC'); // 'Luned\u00EC' expect(words(`${nfcStr} 18 Set`)).toEqual([nfcStr, '18', 'Set']); expect(words(`${nfdStr} 18 Set`)).toEqual([nfdStr, '18', 'Set']); // This test case should pass. // (as-is) failure → ['Lunedi', '18', 'Set'] ← the accent is dropped }); ``` I view this as a correctness issue rather than a mere compatibility one—in any tokenizer, a combining mark inherently belongs to the letter it modifies. For this reason, I'd lean toward fixing both. I intentionally left src/string/words.ts untouched in this PR to keep the scope focused, but I'm happy to extend the fix (along with matching tests and doc updates) if the maintainers agree. ## Conclusion `src/string/words` can follow the es-toolkit team policy (ideally, I'd love to see it updated too!). However, since `compat` needs to stay compatible with `lodash`, shouldn't we definitely update `compat`? 👍

prs.title: fix(dedent): throw a TypeError for a malformed template literal like String.dedent
prs.author: raon0211
prs.request:
fix(dedent): throw a TypeError for a malformed template literal like String.dedent

## Summary

`dedent` accepts any template literal today, even one whose opening or closing line has content. The [TC39 `String.dedent` proposal](https://tc39.es/proposal-string-dedent/) rejects such templates with a `TypeError` (`RemoveOpeningAndClosingLines`), so code that works with `dedent` today would break once it is switched to `String.dedent`.

This PR makes the tagged-template and composed-tag paths follow the proposal: the opening line (right after the opening backtick) and the closing line (right before the closing backtick) may contain only whitespace. Otherwise a `TypeError` is thrown.

```ts
dedent`hello
  world
`;
// TypeError: Invalid opening line.

dedent`
  hello
  world`;
// TypeError: Invalid closing line.
```

## Changes

- Add `assertTemplateShape`, which inspects only the static parts of the template (`strings[0]` and `strings[strings.length - 1]`), so interpolated values never affect the check. It runs for both `` dedent`…` `` and `dedent(tagFn)`.
- Like the proposal, a template with no newline at all, one that starts with `${…}`, or one that ends with `${…}` right before the closing backtick also throws.
- `dedent(str)` with a plain string is unchanged; `String.dedent` only defines the tag form.
- One deliberate difference from the proposal: an opening line that contains only whitespace (e.g. trailing spaces after the opening backtick) is still accepted, as before. The proposal throws there. Being more lenient keeps every template that `String.dedent` accepts working here, while avoiding a runtime error caused by invisible whitespace.
- The error messages mirror core-js's `String.dedent` polyfill (`Invalid opening line` / `Invalid closing line`).
- Docs (`en`, `ko`, `ja`, `zh_hans`) describe the required shape and gain a Throws section.

## Tests

Added to `src/string/dedent.spec.ts`:

- whitespace-only opening line is still accepted
- opening line with content, template with no newline, template starting with an interpolation → `TypeError`
- closing line with content, template ending with an interpolation → `TypeError`
- plain-string form is not checked
- composed tag function throws for the same shapes

## Validation

- `yarn vitest run src/string` → 23 files, 225 tests passed
- `yarn eslint` on touched files → clean
- `yarn tsc --noEmit` → clean

## Comparison with core-js

Ran the same templates through `core-js@3.50.0` (`core-js/full/string/dedent`) and this implementation. All content-on-opening/closing-line, no-newline, starts-with-`${}` and ends-with-`${}` cases throw in both. Remaining differences:

- Whitespace-only opening line: core-js throws, this PR accepts (deliberate, see above).
- U+2028 / U+2029 as line terminators: core-js treats them as newlines, es-toolkit's `dedent` only understands `\n` (as it already did before this PR).
- core-js inspects `strings.raw`, this PR inspects the cooked strings, so an escaped `\n` written in source counts as a newline here but not in core-js.

## Notes

This is a behavior change for templates that were previously accepted. No usage inside the repo is affected. Related: #2099 aligns interpolation handling with the proposal; this PR is independent of it and touches different parts of `dedent.ts`.

prs.title: fix(dedent): keep interpolated values out of the indentation calculation
prs.author: MFA-G
prs.request:
fix(dedent): keep interpolated values out of the indentation calculation

## Summary

`dedent` currently concatenates the interpolated values into the text **before** computing the common indentation. As a result, any value that contains a line break, or that sits on an indented line, distorts the indentation calculation.

```ts
const value = 'a\nb';

dedent`
  hello ${value}
  world
`;
// actual:   '      hello a\nb\n      world'   ← nothing is dedented at all
// expected: 'hello a\nb\nworld'
```

What happens: after substitution the text contains the line `b`, which has zero indentation, so the common indent becomes `0` and none of the template's own indentation is removed.

The same class of bug hits the composed-tag path (`dedent(tagFn)`): it joins the static parts with `\x00` and dedents the joined string, so a `\x00` that appears in a static part corrupts the split back into parts.

## Changes

- `dedent` now dedents the **static parts** of the template as a unit and substitutes the values afterwards, so an interpolated value can never influence the indentation calculation. This matches the behaviour of [`dedent`](https://github.com/dmnd/dedent) and the [TC39 `String.dedent` proposal](https://github.com/tc39/proposal-string-dedent), where only the template's own strings take part in dedenting.
- The join placeholder is now chosen so that it does not occur in the static parts (it grows from `\x00` until it is unique), which fixes the corrupted round-trip in the composed-tag path.
- Both the tagged-template path and the composed-tag path share the same `dedentParts` helper, so they stay consistent.

Note that an interpolation still counts as ordinary content of its own line, so the leading indentation of a line ending in `${…}` is preserved relative to the rest, e.g.:

```ts
dedent`
  hello
    ${'x'}
`; // 'hello\n  x'
```

## Tests

Added cases to `src/string/dedent.spec.ts`:

- multi-line interpolated value does not affect the common indentation
- indented interpolation keeps its relative indentation
- an interpolated value containing `\x00` round-trips correctly
- a static part containing `\x00` round-trips correctly
- composed tag function with a multi-line interpolation

All four new tagged-template tests fail on `main` and pass with this change.

## Validation

- `yarn vitest run src/string` → 23 files, 222 tests passed
- `yarn lint` → 0 errors
- `yarn tsc --noEmit` → clean
- `yarn prettier --check` on the touched files → clean

Docs (`en`, `ko`, `ja`, `zh_hans`) were updated where they described the old substitute-then-dedent order.

prs.title: fix(compat/words): match emoji sequences, non-ASCII numerals and symbols
prs.author: ssi02014
prs.request:
fix(compat/words): match emoji sequences, non-ASCII numerals and symbols ## Summary `words` in `es-toolkit/compat` matched emoji one code point at a time, matched digits only with `\d`, and did not treat symbols as word characters. As a result emoji sequences were torn apart, non-ASCII numerals vanished, and strings like `a€b` were split at the symbol even though lodash keeps them as one word. This PR makes three changes to the default pattern: 1. **Emoji sequences are matched as one word.** The two bare `\p{Emoji_Presentation}` / `\p{Extended_Pictographic}` alternatives are replaced by an emoji-sequence pattern (`rEmojiPict`, `rEmojiAtom`, `rEmojiSeq`): regional indicator pairs, keycaps, and pictograph + modifier + tag, joined by ZWJ. 2. **`rMisc` is widened to numbers and symbols.** It now also matches `\p{N}` and `\p{S}`, which lodash treats as word characters, while excluding Latin-1 non-characters, ASCII digits and pictographs. 3. **The emoji alternative is placed ahead of the digit alternative** so keycaps such as `1️⃣` are not consumed by `\d+` first.
## 1. Non-ASCII numerals [diff-like code block removed] lodash's `rsMisc` is a negated class, so every numeric character that is not an ASCII digit falls into it and becomes part of a word. `es-toolkit/compat` only listed letter categories, so Roman numerals, fractions, Arabic-Indic and full-width digits were dropped. `rMisc` now also matches `\p{N}` (`Nd`, `Nl`, `No`). ASCII digits are excluded with `0-9` so they keep going through the digit and ordinal rules, and Latin-1 numerals such as `²` are excluded through `rNonCharLatin`, as in lodash. | Input | `es-toolkit/compat` (before) | lodash | `es-toolkit/compat` (after) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `words('ⅣⅤ')` | `[]` | `['ⅣⅤ']` | `['ⅣⅤ']` | | `words('⅓')` | `[]` | `['⅓']` | `['⅓']` | | `words('١٢٣')` | `[]` | `['١٢٣']` | `['١٢٣']` | | `words('٣ dogs')` | `['dogs']` | `['٣', 'dogs']` | `['٣', 'dogs']` | | `words('１２３')` | `[]` | `['１２３']` | `['１２３']` | | `words('٠1st')` | `['1st']` | `['٠', '1st']` | `['٠', '1st']` | | `words('٢nd')` | `['nd']` | `['٢nd']` | `['٢nd']` | | `words('x²')` | `['x']` | `['x']` | `['x']` |
## 2. Symbols as word characters The same `rMisc` change also adds `\p{S}` (`Sc`, `Sm`, `So`, `Sk`). lodash treats every symbol outside its ASCII/Latin-1 ranges as a word character, so `a€b` and `ⓐⓑ` are single words there. `es-toolkit/compat` treated symbols as neither word nor separator, which silently split the surrounding letters. Two groups of symbols are excluded from `rMisc`: - Latin-1 symbols (`°`, `±`, `¢`, ...) through `rNonCharLatin`, which lodash never treats as part of a word. - Pictographs, through `rEmojiPict`, so that they are matched by the emoji rule below instead of being glued onto a word. | Input | `es-toolkit/compat` (before) | lodash | `es-toolkit/compat` (after) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `words('a€b')` | `['a', 'b']` | `['a€b']` | `['a€b']` | | `words('a→b')` | `['a', 'b']` | `['a→b']` | `['a→b']` | | `words('ⓐⓑ')` | `[]` | `['ⓐⓑ']` | `['ⓐⓑ']` | | `words('10°')` | `['10']` | `['10']` | `['10']` |
## 3. Emoji sequences ```ts // A character that renders as an emoji. const rEmojiPict = '(?:\\p{Emoji_Presentation}|\\p{Extended_Pictographic})'; // Optional variation selector (U+FE0F) and skin tone modifier. (`☝🏻`, `❤️`) const rEmojiMod = '\\uFE0F?\\p{Emoji_Modifier}?'; // Tag characters. They are invisible and attach attributes to the preceding // emoji, e.g. the subdivision flags. (`🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿`) const rEmojiTag = '[\\u{E0020}-\\u{E007F}]*'; const rEmojiAtom = '(?:' + [ // A pair of regional indicators. (`🇰🇷`) '\\p{Regional_Indicator}{2}', // A digit, `#` or `*`, an optional variation selector, and U+20E3. (`1️⃣`) `[${rNumber}#*]\\uFE0F?\\u20E3`, // A pictograph with optional modifier and tags. (`🚀`, `👋🏽`, `❤️`) `${rEmojiPict}${rEmojiMod}${rEmojiTag}`, ].join('|') + ')'; // Atoms joined by zero-width joiners form one emoji. (`👨‍👩‍👧`) const rEmojiSeq = `${rEmojiAtom}(?:\\u200D${rEmojiAtom})*`; ``` An atom is a regional indicator pair, a keycap, or a pictograph with an optional variation selector, skin tone modifier and tag sequence. A sequence is one or more atoms joined by ZWJ (`U+200D`). Note that `rEmojiMod` makes both the variation selector and the modifier optional on their own, so `❤️`, `👋🏽` and `☝️🏽` are all covered by one expression. | Input | `es-toolkit/compat` (before) | lodash | `es-toolkit/compat` (after) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `words('family 👨‍👩‍👧')` | `['family', '👨', '👩', '👧']` | `['family', '👨‍👩‍👧']` | `['family', '👨‍👩‍👧']` | | `words('wave 👋🏽')` | `['wave', '👋', '🏽']` | `['wave', '👋🏽']` | `['wave', '👋🏽']` | | `words('flag 🇰🇷')` | `['flag', '🇰', '🇷']` | `['flag', '🇰🇷']` | `['flag', '🇰🇷']` | | `words('🕵🏻‍♂️')` | `['🕵', '🏻', '♂']` | `['🕵🏻‍♂️']` | `['🕵🏻‍♂️']` | | `words('☀️ sun')` | `['☀', 'sun']` | `['☀️', 'sun']` | `['☀️', 'sun']` |
## 4. Rule order ```ts function getUnicodeWordPattern(): RegExp { if (rUnicodeWord == null) { rUnicodeWord = RegExp( [ ... `${rNumber}*(?:1ST|2ND|3RD|(?![123])${rNumber}TH)(?=\\b|[a-z_])`, `${rNumber}*(?:1st|2nd|3rd|(?![123])${rNumber}th)(?=\\b|[A-Z_])`, // Placed before the digit rule so that keycaps (`1️⃣`) are not consumed by `\d+` first. rEmojiSeq, `${rNumber}+`, ].join('|'), 'gu' ); ```

They come from lodash's Latin-only ranges rather than from a design decision, and following them would produce results that are wrong for the input. | Input | `es-toolkit/compat` (after) | lodash | Why | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | `words('1️⃣')` | `['1️⃣']` | `['1', '️⃣']` | lodash splits a keycap into the digit and a leftover enclosing mark. | | `words('🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿')` | `['🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿']` | `['🏴', '󠁧', '󠁢', '󠁥', '󠁮', '󠁧', '󠁿']` | lodash emits each invisible tag character as its own word. | | `words('µm')` | `['µm']` | `['m']` | `µ` is a letter (`Ll`); lodash drops it only because it sits in the Latin-1 range. | | `words('©2024')` | `['©', '2024']` | `['2024']` | `©` and `®` are pictographs and stay emoji, as in `es-toolkit` and the previous `compat` implementation. lodash drops them as Latin-1 non-characters. | | `words('ПриветМир')` | `['Привет', 'Мир']` | `['ПриветМир']` | Camel case is split with `\p{Lu}` / `\p{Ll}` in every script, not only Latin.
